villagers.role: Mayor, and chair of nearly every committee
greet: Ah, {name}! Splendid timing. I was just about to start a meeting with myself.
Good morning! The Committee for Mornings has declared this one adequate.
Every week something in this valley mends itself. Well. You mend it. I take the minutes.
I've misplaced my reading glasses. They're on my head, aren't they? Splendid.
The square sounds different lately. Busier. I keep stopping just to listen.
Did you know the town charter is two hundred and twelve pages? I've read it eleven times. For fun.
Mind the puddle by the notice board. It has been tabled for discussion.
Bramblebrook is waking up, {name}. I can feel it. I've started a committee about the feeling.

thanks.loved: Oh! Oh, this is splendid. Truly splendid. I'm entering it into the minutes as a historic gift.
thanks.liked: How thoughtful! The town thanks you. Well, I thank you, on behalf of the town.
thanks.neutral: Ah, a gift! I'll find it a place. Possibly a filing cabinet.
thanks.disliked: That is... certainly a thing. I'll refer it to a subcommittee. A distant one.

requests.say: The Committee for Tidy Verges wants the square's planters filled. Six wildflowers would be splendid. It's been on the agenda for eight years.
I promised Gran Clementine wheat for the Founders' Loaf. I promised it last week. Ten wheat would save my reputation.
A loose flagstone ambushed me outside the town hall. Four stone blocks, please, before it strikes again.
The notice board fell over mid-vote. The motion carried. The board did not. Ten planks, please.
For the bridge celebrations I'd like reed garlands, like in the old photographs. Twelve river reeds. It's in the minutes!
Splendid news: the council has voted you the old allotment by the hedge! I only need two crates for the town archive. It lives in shoeboxes.
The Fair committee wants a centerpiece for Founders' Day. One Celebration Cake. I've written CAKE on the agenda in capitals.
The town hall door needs a chime. Visitors knock, I panic, and I hide under the desk. Two shell chimes would help.
When the bell rings again it deserves a new rope, and the vigil needs candles. One bell rope, four candles. History is watching, {name}!

scene.say: Ah, {name}. You've caught me minuting.
Oakley's desk is buried in notebooks. Every spine is labeled with a date, in very tidy handwriting.
Every meeting since I took office. Even the ones where only I turned up.
Especially those, actually. Somebody has to write down that we tried.
What happens at a meeting of one?
Mostly I second my own motions. It's very efficient. Slightly lonely.
But now there are actual events to minute! Splendid. Pass me that pencil.
In the town hall corridor hang portraits of every mayor of Bramblebrook. The last frame is empty.
Mayor Thistlewood built the square. Mayor Pell dug the well. Mayor Ashby had a truly magnificent mustache.
And Mayor Oakley presided over eight years of things quietly falling down.
I'd rather that frame stayed empty than said 'He meant well.'
You kept the town together.
Did I? I kept the minutes together. It's not quite the same.
Still. Since you arrived, the minutes have been rather exciting to write.

reply.say: Then I'll need to stand up straighter. Splendid. Terrifying, but splendid.
Mayor Ashby's mustache had its own committee. I cannot compete.

scene.say: {name}, I've been rereading the old minutes. The ones from before the bell went quiet.
Do you know what nobody ever wrote down? Who the mayor was. Not once.
They wrote who brought the pie. Who mended the gate. Whose goat ate the agenda.
A town doesn't remember its mayors, it turns out. It remembers its Tuesdays.
So I've decided to be a good Tuesday. A splendid, ordinary, well-minuted Tuesday.
That sounds like a fine thing to be.
Doesn't it? I've minuted that you agreed. Unanimous!
The empty frame in the town hall isn't empty anymore.
Inside is a crayon drawing by Pip: the whole valley at the Fair. In one corner, very small, a man holds a notebook.
I asked Pip for a portrait and got a town. I think that's correct, actually.
Look, there you are, by the bridge. You're in the minutes now, {name}. Permanently.
The council has also voted you a small token of thanks. Unanimously. I was the council. Splendid!

greet: Morning, {name}! I've counted eleven customers already. Well, nine. Ledger came in twice.
Did you hear? No? Come closer. Oh, I've forgotten. It'll come back to me!
Ledger's asleep on the till again. That's where the warm coins are.
Sales are up, gossip is up, and Ledger is up on the top shelf. Good day all round!
There's more chatter in the square than there's been in years. I'm writing it all down.
Funny how a valley goes quiet so long you forget it ever hummed. Listen to it now!
If you're buying, I'm smiling. If you're browsing, I'm still smiling. Slightly less.
Ledger says hello. He says it with his eyes. Very expressive, for a cat.

thanks.loved: Oh, {name}! That's going straight in the ledger under 'Best Things That Happened Today'!
thanks.liked: How lovely! One gift, received with thanks. I'm writing it down.
thanks.neutral: Oh, a gift! I'll put it on the shelf. Ledger may sit on it.
thanks.disliked: Ah. Hmm. I'll file that under 'Miscellaneous', page ninety.

requests.say: Customers keep asking for carrots and I keep saying 'tomorrow'. Six carrots would make an honest woman of me.
Ledger has been staring at me. It's a fish stare. Four minnows, please, before he files a complaint.
I'm out of parcel twine and tying things up with my hair ribbons. Five rolls of twine, please!
Mossy Woods hampers are my bestseller, when I have any. Eight wild berries and five mushrooms, please!
Fresh eggs! Everyone's asking. Bring me six and I'll write your name in the ledger in gold ink.
My shopping baskets have gone missing. One was last seen with Ledger inside it. Three woven baskets, please.
Strawberries are back! People will queue. People will gossip in the queue. Six strawberries, please.
Two jars of strawberry jam for the front window. Not for sale. Just for making people come inside.
I'd love a sea glass necklace for the display case. It's for looking at. And maybe for wearing on Sundays.

scene.say: Behind the counter, Hazel keeps a second ledger. It's older than the shop's, with a red ribbon for a bookmark.
Don't tell anyone. This is the important one.
Every birthday in Bramblebrook. Tobin's, Oakley's, Pip's. Even Ledger's, though he lies about his age.
Nobody should have a birthday that nobody notices. So I notice. Professionally.
Now then. When's yours, {name}? Don't fib. I'll find out anyway.

reply.say: Written in pen! You're official now. Expect cake, and a great deal of fuss.
Oh, I do love a challenge. I'll have it by Friday.

scene.say: {name}, can I show you something sad? Only a little sad. Tea-sized.
Hazel opens the birthday ledger to a page with one name circled twice: Wren Bramble.
I've marked eight of her birthdays since she left. I still buy a candle every year.
Silly, isn't it? Lighting a candle for someone who isn't there to blow it out.
It doesn't sound silly.
No. It doesn't, does it? Thank you.
Right! Enough of that. Ledger, stop eating the receipts.
People think I count things because I'm nosy. I am. But that's not why.
The winter the bell cracked, the shop nearly closed. Nobody came in. Nobody needed anything.
So I counted. Jars, buttons, raindrops on the window. If I'd counted it, the day had happened.
Then you turned up, {name}, and I had to buy a bigger ledger.
I don't count raindrops anymore. I count customers. It's much nicer.

reply.say: Number one, obviously. Don't tell Oakley. He thinks he is.
Oh, that's dreadful. I love it. I'm writing it down.

scene.say: Hazel slides a small parcel across the counter, wrapped in old ledger paper.
I've kept a page for you since the day you arrived. Every gift, every favor.
The totals came out very lopsided. In your favor. That won't do at all.
So, a little something to balance the books. Ledger helped wrap it. That's why it's hairy.
Friends, {name}. Written in pen.

greet: Mornin'.
River's talking today. Mostly about you.
Caught a pike once the size of a rowboat. Small rowboat. Still counts.
Water's clearer than it was. Fish noticed first. They always do.
Boot garden's coming on. Planted a wellington. Should flower by spring.
Sit if you like. Don't talk. Fish can hear.
Valley's remembering itself. Slow. Like a river after a dry summer.
Wind's from the west. Means nothing. Thought you'd want to know.

thanks.loved: Hm. Well. That's a fine thing, {name}. A fine thing.
thanks.disliked: ...Wouldn't feed that to a rabbit. Wouldn't give it to one, neither. Thanks, though.

requests.say: Need bait for the morning. Five minnows. Pike like a minnow. So do I, fried.
Boot garden's got two empty beds. Two old boots, please. And three perch for my supper. Not the boots' supper.
Smoking carp tonight. Two of 'em. And a sunfish, for the color. My wife liked the color.
River's open again. Haven't had a trout in eight years. Four, if you'd be so kind.
Old ferry's mooring line rotted through. Two ropes. Not going anywhere. Just like her tied up proper.
Ferryman's supper. Three catfish, three crayfish. Don't ask what's in it. It's catfish and crayfish.
Lost my lucky lure to a pike. Pike's still out there, wearing it. Four new lures, please.
Two pike, two eels. For the river tally. Kept it forty years. Don't like gaps.
River Stew. Two pots. It was Nell's recipe. Mine never tastes right. Maybe yours will.

scene.say: Behind Tobin's cottage, a row of old boots sits in the sun. Each one is full of soil, and something green grows in every one.
Boot garden.
Why boots?
River gives me boots. Never asked for 'em. Seemed rude to throw 'em back.
That one's a fisherman's. That one's a girl's riding boot. Each one walked somewhere, once.
Now they grow mint. Good retirement, for a boot. Here. Worms. Garden's full of 'em.
See the green one at the end? With the marigolds?
That's Nell's. My wife. Wore it down to the ferry every morning for thirty years.
Lost it in the river the spring she passed. Gone, I thought.
Three years later it comes up on my line. Same boot. Same muddy heel.
So I planted marigolds in it. Her favorite. Then I couldn't stop. That's the whole tale.
Not a tall one, that. Only true one I've got.

reply.say: She'd say it was daft. Then she'd water it.
Hm. Don't make a fuss. ...Thank you for listening.

scene.say: Ran the ferry forty years. Bridge put me out of work. Didn't mind. Liked the bridge.
But there's one crossing I never made. Nell wanted to see the sea. We kept saying next year.
Next year's a liar, {name}. Sly old thing.
So here's a tall tale for you, and it's true: tomorrow, I'm going somewhere.
Don't know where. Downriver. Further than the ferry ever went. Nell would laugh.
Don't wait for next year. That's the advice. Took me seventy years to learn it.

reply.say: ...Aye. Bring worms.
Never sent one in my life. Might start. Pip'll show me how.

scene.say: Tobin hands over a battered tackle box. A faded marigold is painted on the lid.
Forty years of hooks. Most of 'em lucky. Some of 'em very lucky.
Nell painted the lid. Said a box should look cheerful even if the fisherman doesn't.
You fish like you listen, {name}. Quiet. Patient. River likes that.
Go on. Take it before I make a speech.

villagers.role: Tinker, keeper of the old forge
greet: Hey, {name}. Mind the soot. Actually, don't bother. It's everywhere.
Fixed a clock this morning. It now runs perfectly, eleven minutes fast. Progress.
If it's broken, I can fix it. If it's not broken, give me a minute.
Hear that? Hammering. Not mine, for once. The whole valley's mending things.
Grandad used to say a cold forge is just a warm one waiting. Took me years to get it.
Coffee's on the anvil. Don't drink it. It's for the anvil.
This valley's starting to sound like a workshop. Highest compliment I've got.
Lost a screw. Found three. Net gain. Good day.

thanks.loved: Oh, that's... yeah. That's really good. Thank you, {name}.
thanks.neutral: Huh. I'll find a use for it. I always do. Eventually.
thanks.disliked: It's sticky. Why is it sticky? Why do people keep giving me sticky things?

requests.say: I'm testing a rock tumbler. Don't ask what for. I don't know yet either. Twelve pebbles, please.
The forge bellows need a new frame. Fifteen wood. Oak if you can, but I'm not fussy.
I'm rebuilding the forge chimney one stone block at a time. Six more and it might stop leaning.
If the forge is going to breathe again, it needs coal. And copper to practice on. Ten coal, six copper ore.
Grandad's anvil is iron, so I trust iron. Eight iron ore from the quarry, please.
Twenty iron nails. I could make them myself, but then who would I complain to?
My quench bucket sprang a leak. Ironic, for a tinker. One copper bucket and two iron bars, please.
I want to try silversmithing. Grandad never did. Six silver ore and two sky crystals from the deep mine.
Six gold ore and two obsidian. I'm making something for the bell tower. Don't ask. It's a surprise.

scene.say: In the middle of the forge sits an anvil, worn smooth as a river stone.
Grandad's. He shod every horse in the valley on this. Mended every gate.
When the forge went cold, people told me to sell it. Good iron, they said.
It is good iron. That's exactly why I didn't.
It's beautiful.
It's a lump. But it's my lump.
See that dent on the horn? Most people think it's a flaw.
I was six. Dropped a hammer on it. Cried for an hour because I thought I'd broken it.
Grandad just laughed and said, 'Now it's got your mark on it too.'
Every time I work on the horn, I hit that dent. Like he's still checking my work.
Don't tell anyone I said something sentimental. I have a reputation.

reply.say: Good. I'd hate to have to make you a thank-you present.
You wouldn't. ...You would. Ugh. Fine.

scene.say: Can I tell you something, {name}? I nearly left. The year before you came.
Had a job lined up in the city. Fixing machines nobody would ever thank me for.
Packed my tools. Got as far as the door. Then I looked back at the anvil.
Couldn't do it. Felt like leaving someone alone in the dark.
Now the forge is lit and I know why I stayed. It was never about the metal. It's who comes through the door.
Which is mostly you. Covered in mud. Asking for nails.
Mira presses something into your hands. It's still warm from the forge.
Iron sprinkler. Made it on Grandad's anvil. Hit the dent twice, for luck.
Stamped the Ashgrove mark on the bottom. And next to it, yours. I made one up.
It's a turnip. Don't argue. You're very turnip-shaped as a person, {name}. Dependable.
That's a compliment. It's the best one I've got.

greet: Come in, come in. The kettle's just boiled. It always has, when you arrive.
Flour on my nose? I know. I leave it there. It keeps people honest.
You look peaky, {name}. Have a scone. Have two. I'm not asking.
Ovens warm and the valley waking. That's all an old woman needs.
I've seen this valley sleep before, dear. It always wakes up. Usually hungry.
My knees say rain. My knees are right about half the time, same as the almanac.
Wren always said you can tell a gardener by their fingernails. Let's see yours. Hm. Passable.
Mind the cat on the step. It's Hazel's. It thinks it's mine.

thanks.loved: Oh, my dear. You remembered. Come here and let me pinch your cheek.
thanks.liked: Lovely. That'll go into something delicious. Thank you, pet.
thanks.neutral: How kind. I'll find a use for it. I always do.
thanks.disliked: Hm. My mother taught me to say thank you for everything. So: thank you.

requests.say: My flour bin's emptier than a Sunday street. Twelve wheat, dear, and there's a warm loaf in it for you.
Clover tea for my knees and wildflowers for the counter. Six clover and four wildflowers. The knees are the urgent part.
Thursday is pasty day. Five potatoes and four carrots, and I'll save you the crimpiest one.
Ten wild berries from Mossy Woods. Wren and I used to eat more than we picked. Don't you dare.
Ten eggs, please. I've a sponge to make, and Hazel's hens have gone on strike.
Custard! Four milk and six eggs. Don't tell Hazel. She'll want the recipe, and then she'll want to sell it.
The orchard's fruiting again! Eight apples and six pears. I want to bake until the windows steam.
Honey and cherries. Four combs and six cherries. There's a tart I haven't made in eight years. It's time.
Two apple pies, made by you. Wren always called my pie 'adequate'. I'd like to know what she'd say about yours.

scene.say: Gran sets down a faded photograph: two girls on one bicycle, both laughing. One wears a flowerpot for a hat.
That's me in front, pedaling. That's Wren behind, steering. Badly.
We rode it into Lily Pond the summer we were nine. Twice. The second time on purpose.
She wore that flowerpot all summer. Said it was a helmet for her ideas.
What happened to the bicycle?
Still in the pond. Tobin's fished out half of it. He's waiting on the other wheel.
Gran presses two warm rolls into your hands, as if the story needed a snack.
Sit with me a minute, {name}. My hands want kneading and my mouth wants talking.
When we were girls, Wren grew the wheat and I baked it. First loaf of every harvest, split down the middle.
Sixty-odd years, we never missed one. Then she went off to listen for that bell.
I still bake the first loaf every harvest. I still cut it in two.
Half for me. Half wrapped up on the shelf. Just in case.
Just in case of what?
Oh, you know. Just in case.
You're a clever one, {name}. So I'll tell you something I haven't said aloud.
Wren never once went anywhere without telling me where. Not once in seventy years.
'Gone to listen for the bell.' That's not a goodbye, dear. That's a riddle. That's Wren all over.
I had a feeling, all these years. Old friends leave crumbs, if you know where to look.
So I kept her half of the loaf on the shelf. Never let it go stale for long.
Now eat your scone. It's getting sentimental in here.
Gran hands you a tin box, its lid soft with flour and fingerprints.
Every recipe I know. Some I made up. Some I pinched from Wren's mother. She'd want them used.
The tart on the last card has no name. Wren and I never could agree on one.
You name it, {name}. You've earned that, and a great deal more.
And a cake for the road. Don't argue with an old woman holding a rolling pin.

reply.say: Ha! Wren would pretend to hate that. Then she'd eat three slices.
Oh, go on with you. ...Write it in pen.

villagers.role: Explorer and mapmaker, age ten and a half
greet: {name}! I mapped the whole meadow! Well, most of it. Sir Hopsalot sat on a corner.
Sir Hopsalot says good morning. He says it with his throat. It's very loud.
Did you know snails have four noses? I didn't either. I made it up. But they COULD.
My map has way fewer 'HERE BE DRAGONS' bits now. You keep fixing them!
Explorers don't have bedtimes. Mum disagrees. Mum is wrong.
Everything's getting un-broken! I have to redraw my map every week. It's the BEST.
Sir Hopsalot is a real knight, you know. I did it with a spoon.
Got a postcard from Dad! It has a whale on it. A drawing of a whale. Still counts.

thanks.loved: WHOA! For me?! This is going in the Museum of Pip! Sir Hopsalot, LOOK!
thanks.liked: Ooh, nice! Thanks, {name}! It's going on my shelf of good stuff.
thanks.neutral: Oh! Um, thanks! I'll find out what it's for. That's what explorers do.
thanks.disliked: Ew. Um. Sir Hopsalot says thank you. I'm not saying anything.

requests.say: Every explorer needs a cairn! Eight pebbles to mark the edge of my map. That's where the Unknown starts!
Sir Hopsalot refused his breakfast. He's very particular. Four worms and two snails, for a tasting menu!
My explorer hat needs feathers. Three of them! A hat with no feathers is just a hat.
I want Sir Hopsalot to meet a bullfrog. For diplomacy. I'll let it go after. Pinky promise!
I'm mapping Mossy Woods and I need specimens! Six acorns and three ferns. For SCIENCE.
Is it true there are dinosaur bones in the Old Quarry?! Bring me a fossil. Any size. A tiny dinosaur still counts.
Hazel says there are glowing mushrooms down the mine. I'm not allowed in. So you have to bring me three. Please!
Dad always sends me things from the sea. I want to send him something from OUR sea. Two starfish and six shells!
Eagle feathers would make my hat a proper expedition hat. Two, in case Sir Hopsalot wants one.

scene.say: Pip unrolls a map almost as tall as Pip. Every inch is labeled in wobbly capitals.
This is the whole valley! I drew it. That's the farm. That's you, the stick person with the hoe.
And that's Lily Pond. It's Sir Hopsalot's country. He's in charge. Well, he's a knight. He's working up.
All the gray bits are broken places. I'm gonna color them in when they're fixed.
That's a lot of gray.
Not as much as before! You keep giving me coloring to do!
Pip's bedroom wall is covered in postcards. Lighthouses, whales, one very surprised-looking seal.
My dad's a sailor. He's on a big ship that goes everywhere. He sends a postcard from every port.
Forty-one so far! I mark every port on my map, so I always know where he's been.
I don't mind that he's away. Explorers have to explore. I get it. I'm one too.
Only sometimes I wish the postcards were longer. Like, two sentences longer.
What would you want them to say?
Dunno. Maybe 'I saw a map shop and thought of you.' Here, have a feather. I'm being brave.
{name}, I did a brave thing. I wrote Dad a postcard back. A long one.
I told him about the bridge and the forge and the mine and you. It took both sides AND the stamp bit.
I said I'm a real explorer now, because I have a real friend to explore with.
And he wrote back already! It says, 'Coming home for the winter. Draw me a map of everywhere.'
So I have to finish the map! All of it! You have to help!

reply.say: YES! Sir Hopsalot, get your helmet!
He can't. He hops in circles. But he's very confident about it.

scene.say: Pip's map is finished. Every gray bit is colored in, some of them twice.
Dad says it's the best map he's ever seen. And he's seen LOADS. He's a sailor.
I put a star on your farm. Explorers always mark where the treasure is.
And I want you to have this. My lucky compass. It points north. Mostly. Sometimes at snacks.
You're my best expedition partner ever, {name}.
Sir Hopsalot is second. He knows. He's fine about it.

villagers.role: Keeper of the lighthouse on the Point
greet: Tide's turning. So's the day. So, it seems, are you.
The sea said your name this morning. Mostly it says 'hush'. You're an improvement.
Fog on the water. The gulls are gossiping. Worse than Hazel.
Wind from the north. Smells of snow and old promises.
Every night I write the weather in the log. The weather never writes back.
The valley's brighter from up here than it was. I notice. Not much else to do but notice.
Sit. Watch the horizon with me. Only show in town that never repeats.

thanks.loved: ...Well. You've a keeper's eye, {name}. That's rare as calm water.
thanks.liked: Kind of you. The sea's stingy with gifts. You're not.
thanks.neutral: Hm. I'll put it on the shelf with the other mysteries.
thanks.disliked: Too bright. Too cheerful. Give it to someone with less weather in their soul.

requests.say: The stair rail's gone soft as bread. Two ropes and six planks. I'd rather not meet the rocks the quick way.
Driftwood for the stove. Seaweed for the garden I pretend I don't keep. Eight and six.
Haven't fished the cove in years. Pride, mostly. Three crabs and four shrimp, and we'll say no more about it.
Two lanterns for the gallery. Small lights. But a small light is still a promise to someone out there.
Cove Chowder, two bowls. One for me. One for whoever climbs all those stairs to visit. You, usually.
A crystal lamp for the log desk. Some nights my eyes feel older than the sea.

scene.say: Rook's log lies open on the desk. Neat columns: date, weather, ships seen.
Every ship that's passed the Point in thirty years. Names, if I could read them. Guesses, if I couldn't.
'The Gull's Regret.' 'Persistence.' That one I called 'Dumpling'. It was round.
Did any of them know you were watching?
No. That's the job. Watch, so nobody else has to worry.
Lonely work. Good work. Both at once, like most things worth doing.
You want to know why the light went dark? Not the storm. Me.
The night the bell cracked, the wind took the gallery windows. I went up to save the lens.
Had it in my arms. Then the floor tilted, and I had a choice: the lens or the railing.
I chose the railing. The lens went into the cove. I heard it sing on the rocks.
Eight years I've blamed myself for being alive instead of brave.
You chose right.
Aye. That's what the sea keeps telling me. I'm a slow listener.
People ask why I stayed when the light went out. Hazel asks weekly. With biscuits.
A keeper doesn't keep a light, {name}. A keeper keeps watch. The light's just the loud part.
Some nights I'd see a lamp moving, far up in the highlands. Never knew whose.
I'd flash my hand lantern back. Three times. Old sailor's hello.
And sometimes, I swear, it flashed back.

reply.say: Maybe. Two keepers, two hills, one dark valley. Not so lonely, put like that.

choices.t: Did you ever find out who?

reply.say: Some questions are better as lights than answers. ...But I've a guess.

scene.say: Rook opens an old tea tin. Inside are pale, frosted pieces of glass, worn smooth by the tide.
Pieces of the old lens. The sea's been giving them back, one tide at a time.
Took eight years to turn my worst night into something pretty. Patient, the sea.
I want you to have them. You helped me stop listening to the rocks, {name}.
Make something that catches the light. It's all glass ever wanted.

greet: Mm. Morning.
Sheep are well. I'm well. That's the news.
Wind's up. Good. Keeps the flies honest.
You walk louder than a lamb. Getting quieter, though.
Valley's lighter than it was. You can see it from the ridge. More lamps at night.
Brought you nothing. Came to say hello. That's the gift.
Fog on the tops today. Sheep don't mind. Neither do I.

thanks.disliked: Mm. No. But thank you for thinking of me.

requests.say: Carrots. Fifteen. The flock pretend they don't like them. Sheep are liars.
Thyme for the cheese. Eight sprigs. From the upper slopes. The lower ones taste of goat.
Ten heather. For a friend who misses color. Don't ask who.
Three yarn. Winters are long up top. Long enough to knit a whole sheep, nearly.
Two ice perch, three char. The tarn's generous if you're patient. I've no patience left this week.
A picnic on the ridge. Wren, Clementine and me, first in eight years. Two cheeses and four loaves, please.

scene.say: Ingrid walks the flock along the ridge, touching each sheep on the head as it passes.
Thistle. Old Mags. Pudding. Biscuit. Small Biscuit.
You've named them all?
Course. You don't leave a thing unnamed up here. Wind would take it.
That one's Stubborn. She is.
...You can name the next lamb. If you like.

reply.say: Pip's been at you. ...Fine. Sir Woolsalot.
Clover. Good. Plain. She'll wear it well.

scene.say: Lost a lamb once. Storm like the one that cracked the bell. Couldn't see my own hands.
Shouting didn't help. Wind ate it. So I stopped. Stood still. Listened.
Took an hour. Then, one small bleat, under a ledge. Right below my boots.
Most things you lose, you find by going quiet. Took me years to learn it.
Is that why you live up here?
Mm. Up here it's quiet enough to hear what matters.
{name}. Sit. I owe you a story. Short one. I'm no good at long.
Eight winters back, a friend went up the Highland Road. Then the slide came down behind.
Couldn't come back. Wouldn't, maybe. Asked me to tell no one. Not until the bell could ring.
I kept that promise. Through every worried face in the valley. Every one.
Some nights I hated it. Some nights I was proud. Mostly both.
Maybe you know who I mean by now. If not, you will. Either way, I'm sorry I couldn't say.

choices.t: You kept your word. That matters.

reply.say: ...Mm. Thank you. That helps more than you'd think.
No. You'd have told everyone by teatime. That's why you're good for this valley.

scene.say: Ingrid hands you a folded bundle: a scarf, thick and slightly lopsided, the color of heather.
Knitted it on the long nights. Dropped a stitch or ten. Didn't unpick them.
Mistakes make it warmer. That's what I tell myself.
Wool and yarn too. For your own long nights. You'll have them. Everyone does.
You're welcome on the ridge, {name}. Any time. That's not a thing I say.

greet: Ah. The heir. Your carrots are slouching, {name}. Have a word with them.
Eight years of mountain air and I come home to find you've done all my chores. Rude.
Morning. The tomatoes and I have been talking. They have notes.
Clementine has fed me four times today. I'm hiding in the potato patch.
Funny thing about a valley. You leave it dim and come back to find it humming.
Don't fuss. I'm old, not fragile. Fragile things don't last eight winters on a mountain.
Sky's clear tonight. I've mapped it twice already. Still there. Good.
You've done well with the place. Don't let it go to your head. Let it go to the soil.

thanks.loved: Now that's a proper gift. You've been paying attention. Dangerous habit. Keep it up.
thanks.liked: Very nice. I'll pretend I'm not pleased. I'm pleased.
thanks.neutral: Hm. Thank you, {name}. It'll find a use, or a compost heap.
thanks.disliked: Absolutely not. I'll give it to Clementine. She'll pretend to like it. She's better at that than me.

requests.say: My old herb beds have been sulking for eight years. Three grow tonics and a stern word should sort them out.
Two pumpkins. One for Clementine's pie. One to sit on. I've missed a good garden seat.
Up there I grew herbs in teacups. I want a proper bed again: six thyme, six heather, six fern. The east bed's yours too.
Three sunflowers. They follow the sun all day. I spent eight years following stars. We understand each other.
Pip's taking over the observatory star charts, and the old glass is cracked. One good lens, please. The lighthouse kind will do.
Moonbloom. My mother's flower. Grow me three and I'll admit you're a better gardener than me. Nearly.

scene.say: Come here. No, closer. Kneel. Your knees will survive.
Put your hand flat on the soil. Now hush. Not your mouth. Your head.
You wait. A breeze moves through the beans. Somewhere, a leaf turns over.
Hear that? The beans are thirsty. They're being polite about it. Beans are polite.
I didn't hear anything.
Good. That's step one. Most people only hear themselves. Step two takes about forty years.
Plants don't talk, {name}. Don't look at me like I'm mad. They don't talk. They lean.
Toward the light. Away from the wind. Toward each other when the ground is poor.
Learn to read a lean and you'll know a garden better than its gardener does.
Took me eight years on a mountain to notice people lean too.
This whole valley's been leaning toward you since you came. Did you notice?

reply.say: Liar. But a kind one. You'll learn.

choices.t: I thought it leaned toward cake.

reply.say: Also true. Clementine's cake has its own gravity.

scene.say: Everyone asks why I left. Nobody asks why I stayed up there. You haven't either. I like that.
I went for star-iron. Practical. Then the road came down and I had to be patient. I'm dreadful at patient.
So I listened. To the sky, mostly. Turns out stars lean too. Very slowly.
At night I'd look down at the valley and count the lights. Fewer every year.
Then one spring, a new one. Out at the old farm. Somebody had moved in.
That's when I knew I could wait a bit longer. Somebody was listening down there.
Don't you dare cry. I'll start, and I haven't the eyelashes for it.
Wren walks you to the old east bed. The soil is dark, and the morning is very quiet.
One day, many years from now, and I do mean many, this farm will be yours. Truthfully? It already is.
Every plant here knows your footsteps. That doesn't happen to just anybody.
Here. Tonics, my own recipe. Don't tell Hazel. She'll put a price on them.
Now go and listen to something, {name}. I've a nap to take, and the beans won't wait.

greet: Saffi's Wandering Wares! Everything priced to move, darling. Mostly because I move.
Ah, my favorite customer! I say that to everyone. This time I very nearly mean it.
Fresh from over the hills! Well. Over some hills. Hills are hills.
Today's bargain: everything. Tomorrow's bargain: also everything. Buy today anyway.
The cart's freshly painted and the prices are freshly fair. Look closely. Fair-ish.
This valley gets brighter every time I roll through. Bright valleys buy more. I'm a fan.
sold: Sold! A pleasure doing business. Mostly my pleasure, but some of it's yours.
Excellent choice! I'd have bought it myself if I didn't already own it.
Wrapped, done, yours! No refunds, but plenty of compliments.
You drive a hard bargain. Well, you paid full price. But you LOOKED like you'd haggle.
bought: Ooh, quality goods! I'll sell these in the next valley for... well. That's my business.
Done and done! A fair price, give or take a take.
I'll take them! You've an eye for things that sell. Ever thought of getting a cart?
Lovely work! Next time bring twice as many. I'll pretend to be surprised.
